gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Apex 300's headline 0 ms UPS applies only to two front outlets in 240 V mode, and that in ordinary 120 V mode it is a 20 ms unit that StorageReview measured at 16 ms, which is no faster than the Apex 200's ≤15 ms (a mode that is off by default); none says either that the 7,680 W and 5,400 W 'Lifting Power' figures are not surge ratings.
standout_why: I compared against BLUETTI's Apex 200 vs Apex 300 blog (Nov 5, 2026, cited) and the cited Apex 200 and Apex 300 product pages. The blog states '0ms UPS Response Time' for the Apex 300 with no condition, and it already flags that the cycle-life thresholds differ (70% vs 80%), so that point is not new. The Apex 300 page lists '0ms or 20ms switching' without saying which outlets or mode give which, and it lists 7,680 W 'Lifting Power' without defining it. The Apex 200 page lists 5,400 W 'Lifting Power' and ≤15 ms. None of these pages gives a measured transfer time, a surge figure that can be compared, measured usable Wh, or AC charging watts for each cable. ChatGPT's answer leaves UPS out entirely and assumes 85% usable energy.
decides: The Apex 300 stays the pick for any 240 V load. For a shopper with only 120 V essentials, UPS speed is not a reason to pay more: in 120 V mode the Apex 300 is a 20 ms unit (16 ms measured), the same class as the Apex 200's ≤15 ms. Compared standalone, the output gap is 640 W (3,840 W vs 3,200 W), not 240 W, because the Apex 200's 3,600 W needs an expansion battery or live input. On BLUETTI's store today the Apex 200 is $400 cheaper ($1,099 vs $1,499), so it gets stronger for 120 V-only backup.

findings.value: 0 ms only on two front outlets in 240 V mode; 20 ms in 120 V mode; measured 16 ms

The BLUETTI product page itself lists '0ms or 20ms switching' with no condition.
